# Iterated Function Systems (IFS)

An IFS is a finite set of contractive transformations (usually affine maps). Iterating them randomly produces a fractal attractor. When the set of maps is closed under a symmetry group, the attractor inherits that symmetry.

This connects directly to the fractal constructions you may have seen in the Fractals module (self-similar shapes built by repeatedly replacing a figure with smaller copies of itself).

## Simple symmetric IFS in R

The following three maps generate a symmetric Sierpinski-like gasket with rotational symmetry of order 3.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-cap: "IFS attractor with order-3 rotational symmetry"

# Three contractive maps (scale 0.5 toward the vertices)
maps <- list(
  function(p) 0.5 * p + c(0, 0),
  function(p) 0.5 * p + c(0.5, 0),
  function(p) 0.5 * p + c(0.25, sqrt(3)/4)
)

n <- 25000
pts <- matrix(0, n, 2)
pts[1,] <- c(0.3, 0.3)

for (i in 2:n) {
  f <- sample(maps, 1)[[1]]
  pts[i,] <- f(pts[i-1,])
}

df <- as.data.frame(pts)
names(df) <- c("x","y")
ggplot(df, aes(x,y)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.2, alpha = 0.4, color = "purple") +
  coord_fixed() + theme_void()
```

## p5.js: live IFS with adjustable symmetry

```{=html}
<div id="ifs-sketch"></div>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/p5@1.9.0/lib/p5.min.js"></script>
<script>
new p5((p) => {
  let x = 0, y = 0;
  let n = 4; // order of symmetry
  p.setup = () => {
    p.createCanvas(400, 400);
    p.background(255);
    p.strokeWeight(0.8);
  };
  p.draw = () => {
    p.translate(200, 200);
    for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
      // Randomly apply a scaled rotation toward a vertex
      let k = p.floor(p.random(n));
      let angle = k * p.TWO_PI / n;
      let vx = 120 * p.cos(angle);
      let vy = 120 * p.sin(angle);
      x = (x + vx) * 0.5;
      y = (y + vy) * 0.5;
      p.stroke(80, 120, 200, 120);
      p.point(x, y);
    }
  };
}, document.getElementById("ifs-sketch"));
</script>
```

# A Simple Design Procedure

1. **Choose the desired symmetry group**  
   Decide on rotational order \( n \) or full dihedral \( D_n \). This is the same vocabulary as Document 1.

2. **Select a fundamental domain**  
   Pick a small set of “seed” points or a basic shape that will be copied by the group actions.

3. **Define contractive maps that respect the group**  
   For each group element \( g \), include a map of the form  
   \[ f_g(p) = s \cdot g(p) + t \]  
   where \( s < 1 \) is a scale factor and \( t \) is a translation.  
   The collection \( \{f_g\} \) must be closed under the group action if you want the full symmetry.

4. **Iterate randomly**  
   Start from any point and repeatedly apply a randomly chosen map. After discarding the first few hundred iterates, plot the remaining points (or color by density).

5. **Tune**  
   Adjust scales, translations, and the probability of each map. Small changes produce large visual differences while the symmetry is preserved.

## Example: adding reflections

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-cap: "Dihedral version (rotations + reflections)"

# Maps that include both rotations and a reflection
reflect <- function(p) c(p[1], -p[2])
base_maps <- list(
  function(p) 0.5 * p + c(0.4, 0),
  function(p) 0.5 * p + c(-0.2, 0.35)
)

n_iter <- 20000
pts <- matrix(0, n_iter, 2)
pts[1,] <- c(0.1, 0.1)

for (i in 2:n_iter) {
  f <- sample(base_maps, 1)[[1]]
  p <- f(pts[i-1,])
  if (runif(1) < 0.5) p <- reflect(p)   # randomly apply reflection
  # also rotate by 120° occasionally for order 3
  if (runif(1) < 0.3) {
    th <- 2*pi/3
    R <- matrix(c(cos(th), -sin(th), sin(th), cos(th)), 2, 2)
    p <- as.numeric(R %*% p)
  }
  pts[i,] <- p
}

df <- as.data.frame(pts)
names(df) <- c("x","y")
ggplot(df, aes(x,y)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.15, alpha = 0.35, color = "darkgreen") +
  coord_fixed() + theme_void()
```

# Connection to Classic Fractals

- Sierpinski triangle / carpet → special cases of the above procedure with particular scales and translations.
- Koch curve, dragon curve, etc. can be rewritten as IFS and then symmetrized by adding the group actions.
- The same design steps work whether you are building a deterministic L-system or a random IFS.

Once you have a set of maps that carry a symmetry, every iterate (and therefore the whole attractor) respects that symmetry. That is the bridge from Document 1 into generative fractal design.
